passage: Thursday after school, outside the tuition centre in the colony, Kabir tapped his phone. "We're all bunking. Mall, then the arcade. Uday, you in? Or are you going to run to tuition like a good boy?" A couple of them smirked. Uday's chest went tight. He didn't want to go; he had a test the next day. But the thought of the group chat filling with jokes about him made his mouth say, "Yeah, sure." At the mall he kept checking the time and laughed a beat too late at everything. That night he admitted to himself that he had been scared, plain and simple. Next day he told Harsha, who groaned, "Me too. I hate saying no." They practised at lunch: "Nah, I'll pass, catch you later." It sounded clumsy and easy at once.

qa.q: Where did the group go after Kabir said they were bunking?
qa.a: To the mall and then the arcade.

qa.q: Why did Uday say yes even though he didn't want to go?
qa.a: He was afraid of being laughed at and left out. His chest went tight and he imagined the group chat filling with jokes about him.

qa.q: What small steps did Uday take to handle the pressure next time?
qa.a: He admitted the fear was real, found Harsha as an ally who would say no with him, and practised a short reply like "Nah, I'll pass, catch you later."

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt when Uday admitted his fear?
qa.a: Relieved. He groaned and said "Me too," which suggests he felt the same fear of saying no and was glad not to be alone.

grounding: The protagonist goes along out of fear of ridicule, then admits the fear, finds an ally and practises a short reply.

passage: Dear diary, Seema here, and I'm in a weird mood. Today at break I called Jomon a baby, again, because he wouldn't skip games period to sit on the terrace with us. "Rule follower," I said, and Ria laughed. He went red and walked off to the ground alone. I felt clever for about a minute. Now, sitting here, I keep thinking about how hard I pushed. Why did I need him to come so badly? I think if he had joined, I'd feel less silly for doing it. I do get nervous when someone calmly says no, because it makes me look at my own choice. Tomorrow I might just say sorry, and not drag anyone along. Anyone can pick their own way. 😅

qa.q: What did Seema call Jomon at break?
qa.a: She called him a baby and a rule follower.

qa.q: Why did Seema push Jomon so hard to join, and what does she realise about herself?
qa.a: She realises she wanted him to join so she would feel less silly about her own choice, and that a calm no makes her uneasy and forces her to look at herself.

qa.q: What could Seema do the next day?
qa.a: Say sorry to Jomon, accept that he can choose differently, and stop dragging others into what she does.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt when Seema called him a baby?
qa.a: Embarrassed and hurt. He went red and walked off alone, though he still kept his choice.

grounding: The protagonist looks down on rule-following friends, then sees her own insecurity and resolves to respect different choices.

passage: I'm Kishore, and for two months I lied for Gurleen. She was leaving school early to ride pillion with an older boy's friend who drove too fast, no helmets, and each time I told the teacher she had a fever. I thought that was what a loyal friend does. Then one Monday she came in with a scraped arm and a limp and laughed it off. My stomach dropped. I finally saw that I hadn't been protecting Gurleen; I'd been protecting the thing that might really hurt her. That evening I told her I couldn't cover for her any more and that I was going to speak to her aunt. She was furious for days. Then, quietly, she said, "I'm glad somebody did."

qa.q: What did Kishore tell the teacher each time Gurleen left early?
qa.a: That she had a fever.

qa.q: Why did Kishore's stomach drop when he saw Gurleen's scraped arm?
qa.a: He realised his covering was not protecting his friend but helping her get hurt, and he understood his loyalty had been aimed at the wrong thing.

qa.q: What would you advise someone in Kishore's position?
qa.a: Be loyal to the friend's wellbeing, not to the risky act, so tell her first and then tell an adult who can help. 🤍

qa.q: How might Gurleen have felt during the days she was furious and after?
qa.a: At first angry and exposed, maybe betrayed. Later her quiet "I'm glad somebody did" shows some relief that someone cared enough to act.

grounding: The protagonist covers for a friend's dangerous rule-breaking, then chooses loyalty to her wellbeing by telling an adult.

passage: On the terrace after the society's Diwali party, Rohan dared everyone to climb onto the water-tank ledge for a photo. Gurleen looked at the drop and said, "I'll pass. I'm going to the swings, anyone want chai afterwards?" Somebody muttered, "Boring." She grinned, shrugged, and walked off without another word. A minute later she heard footsteps. Nilesh caught up, hands in his pockets. "I didn't want to either," he said, "but I wasn't going to be the first to say it." She didn't lecture him. She just said, "Race you to the swing?" Later, when the others climbed down laughing and shaking, she waved them over for chai as well, without any comment.

qa.q: Where did Gurleen go when she refused to climb onto the ledge?
qa.a: To the swings.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh follow Gurleen, and what did he admit?
qa.a: He didn't want to climb either but hadn't wanted to be the first to say so. Gurleen's refusal gave him a way out.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do that kept things friendly after she refused?
qa.a: She said no lightly, didn't lecture Nilesh, and later waved the others over for chai without a comment.

qa.q: How might the others see Gurleen's choice?
qa.a: Some may find it boring, as one muttered. But her cheerful invitation to chai gives them no reason to feel judged, so it may be easier for them to accept it.

grounding: The protagonist refuses peer pressure lightly, another friend follows her, and she stays friendly without preaching.

passage: Elizabeth had chatted with "Ryan" for two weeks in a games forum. He said she was mature for her age and different from everyone. Tonight he wrote, "Send me a picture, just for me. And don't tell your parents, they wouldn't get it." Elizabeth's heart thudded. The flattery had felt warm, but this felt wrong and secret in a way that made her hands cold. She didn't reply. She blocked him, took a screenshot, then sat in the dark on her bed, breathing fast. After a while she walked to the living room and said to her older cousin Anjali, "Can I show you something? I think I did something stupid." Anjali read it, put an arm around her and said, "You did nothing wrong. Let's tell your mum together."

qa.q: What did "Ryan" ask Elizabeth to do in his last message?
qa.a: To send him a picture and not tell her parents.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel as she read the message, and what suggests she trusted her instincts?
qa.a: Scared and uneasy. Her heart thudded and her hands went cold, and she acted on the feeling by not replying, blocking him and taking a screenshot.

qa.q: What would you advise Elizabeth and Anjali to do next?
qa.a: Tell Elizabeth's mum together, keep the screenshot and let the adults help with reporting. Elizabeth should not send anything, and it is not her fault. 🤍

qa.q: How might Anjali see Elizabeth's decision to show her the messages?
qa.a: As brave and sensible. Anjali reassured her that she did nothing wrong and offered to support her when she told her mum.

grounding: An online contact flatters and asks for a photo and secrecy; the protagonist stops, blocks and tells a trusted adult.

passage:
Monday night. Vikas heard whispers through the kitchen door: "the tests," "the fees," "if the shop doesn't pick up." His father's cough sounded worse. At school the equations blurred and he read the same line five times.

Thursday. He found his mother alone. "Mummy, what's going on? I'd rather know." She sat down slowly. Papa was being treated, money was tight, but they had a plan, and Vikas was not to carry it. He asked what he could do. She said, "Take Deepak to school and pick him up."

The next Sunday. Vikas did his homework at the table, dropped Deepak off, and went to play cricket for an hour with friends. It didn't fix the worry. But he could breathe.

qa.q: What did Vikas hear through the kitchen door on Monday night?
qa.a: Whispers about "the tests", "the fees" and "if the shop doesn't pick up".

qa.q: How was Vikas feeling on Monday night and at school, and what shows it?
qa.a: Worried. The equations blurred and he read the same line five times, and his father's cough sounded worse to him.

qa.q: What did Vikas do that helped him and his family, and what should he avoid?
qa.a: He asked what was happening, took on a small job of taking Deepak to school, and kept studying and seeing friends. He should avoid silently carrying adult burdens alone.

qa.q: How might Vikas's mother feel about his question?
qa.a: Probably a mix of worry and relief. She sat down slowly and told him the truth but said he was not to carry the plan, so she wants to protect him.

grounding: A teenager worries about a parent's illness and tight money, asks what is happening and takes small jobs while keeping his life.

passage:
Dear Lokesh,

I have been lying to you for weeks and I hate it. I didn't skip your birthday dinner because of "tuition". I skipped it because Papa's shop has had almost no customers, and I can't afford even the share of the bill. The same with the cricket trip, and the movie. I told everyone I was busy, and I felt like a fraud each time. I was scared you would all look at me differently, or feel sorry for me. Then I saw you looking hurt on Tuesday and thought I owed you the truth. Please don't tell anyone else yet. I'd like to still come to things that cost nothing, like the ground after school. Can we do that?

Shankar

qa.q: Why did Shankar skip Lokesh's birthday dinner?
qa.a: Because Papa's shop has had almost no customers and he could not afford his share of the bill.

qa.q: Why did Shankar hide the real reason from his friends, and what changed his mind?
qa.a: He was scared they would look at him differently or feel sorry for him. Seeing Lokesh look hurt made him feel he owed him the truth.

qa.q: What was wise about Shankar's letter and his request at the end?
qa.a: He chose one trusted friend, stopped pretending, and asked to join things that cost nothing, so he keeps his friendships without lying or spending what he doesn't have.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Probably relieved to know why Shankar kept declining, and perhaps sorry for having been hurt. He may also feel trusted, and he can suggest free plans.

grounding: The protagonist hides his family's money trouble out of shame, then tells one trusted friend the truth.

passage:
Gargi: are you awake
Neelam: yes, what happened?
Gargi: I skipped the school trip again. Mummy had a bad day and I stayed home
Neelam: oh Gargi. That's the third one
Gargi: and I was so angry at her. and then I felt like the worst daughter ever
Neelam: hey
Gargi: I even snapped at her this morning about the water bottle. She just looked at me
Neelam: Being angry and loving her can both be true
Gargi: does that make sense to anyone but me
Neelam: it does. I felt it when my dad was ill
Gargi: you never said
Neelam: I should have. Maybe talk to your school counsellor? And tell Mummy sorry when you're ready
Gargi: ok. thank you didi

qa.q: How many school trips had Gargi missed, according to Neelam?
qa.a: Three, as Neelam says "That's the third one".

qa.q: What is Gargi feeling about her mother's illness, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Anger mixed with guilt. She was very angry that she missed the trip, then felt like the worst daughter, and she snapped about a water bottle.

qa.q: What could Gargi do to handle these mixed feelings without taking them out on her mother?
qa.a: Tell someone safe, like her school counsellor or Neelam, and say sorry to her mother when she is ready. The feelings are normal, and talking helps. 🤍

qa.q: How does Neelam see Gargi's feelings?
qa.a: As normal and understandable. She felt the same when her dad was ill, and she encourages Gargi to talk to a counsellor.

grounding: The protagonist resents a parent's illness limiting her life, then feels guilty; a relative tells her mixed feelings are normal.

passage: I'm Tushar, and I first really noticed my mother, Ganga, when I was fifteen and found her at midnight hemming other people's blouses again. She'd done it for years so I could stay in school, and I'd never once asked how her shoulders felt. That night I said thank you, badly, and she waved it away. I felt warm and heavy at once. I told myself I would become an engineer, earn a lot, and pay it all back. Then one evening, sketching buildings in my notebook, I realised I didn't want to be an engineer; I wanted to be an architect. When I said so, she stopped sewing. "I didn't work for your life to belong to me," she said. Now I cook dinner twice a week and keep drawing.

qa.q: What was Ganga doing at midnight when Tushar noticed her?
qa.a: Hemming other people's blouses.

qa.q: What two feelings did Tushar have after thanking his mother?
qa.a: Warmth and heaviness, meaning gratitude together with the pressure to succeed and repay her.

qa.q: What did Tushar do that was fair to his mother and to himself?
qa.a: He said thanks and took on a real responsibility by cooking dinner twice a week, but he kept drawing instead of giving up his own dream to repay her.

qa.q: How does Ganga see what she has done for Tushar?
qa.a: As a gift, not a debt. She stopped sewing and said she didn't work for his life to belong to her.

grounding: The protagonist sees a parent's sacrifices with gratitude and pressure, thanks her, shares responsibility and keeps his own dream.

passage:
"Manjula, sit with me a moment."
"Amma, it's past eleven."
"Just listen. The loan instalment is due and your father's contract might not be renewed. I don't know how we'll manage. You're the only one who understands me."
"I do listen, Amma. But I don't know what to do about a loan. I'm fourteen."
"I know. I just needed to say it aloud to someone."
"I'm glad you told me. But could you talk to Shreya Masi, or Papa, about the money part? I can sit with you after, and make tea."
Amma was quiet, then reached for her phone. "I'll call Masi in the morning."
Manjula hugged her, proud that she'd been trusted, and tired in her whole body.

qa.q: How old is Manjula?
qa.a: She is fourteen.

qa.q: How does Manjula feel about being told her mother's worries?
qa.a: Proud and burdened. She hugs her mother, glad she was trusted, but feels tired in her whole body and says she doesn't know what to do about a loan.

qa.q: What did Manjula do that helped both her mother and herself?
qa.a: She listened and offered tea, but asked her mother to take the money worries to Shreya Masi or Papa, so adults handle adult matters.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt when Manjula suggested calling Shreya Masi?
qa.a: Probably relieved, if a little guilty. She was quiet, then reached for her phone and said she would call Masi in the morning.

grounding: A parent leans emotionally on the teenager, who supports her but asks that adults handle adult matters.
